introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2025. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 3 » par section (A, B, C, D), ce qui correspond exactement à la consigne imprimée ; la consigne complète est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »), soit 100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter. Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde, puis les questions 1 à 12 réparties en quatre sections de trois questions) : filigranes gcerevision.com ignorés ; aucune question coupée ni illisible, aucune figure ni carte dans le sujet.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune citation ni statistique précise n'est avancée ; les dates, noms, traités et lieux sont ceux de l'historiographie établie, cités de mémoire historique et à faire relire par un historien avant mise en vente.

Question 7 : faits cités de mémoire historique (invitation des sept notables en juin 1688, débarquement de Guillaume d'Orange à Torbay en novembre 1688, fuite de Jacques II en décembre 1688, Déclaration puis Bill of Rights de 1689, Toleration Act 1689, Triennial Act 1694, Banque d'Angleterre 1694, Act of Settlement 1701, bataille de la Boyne 1690, traité de Limerick 1691, massacre de Glencoe 1692, soulèvements jacobites de 1715 et 1745) ; la taille de la flotte et de l'armée hollandaise n'est pas chiffrée.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Discuss the view that "the 1688 revolution in England was glorious and inglorious."

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The revolution of 1688 in England brought about the removal of the Catholic king James II and the arrival, as joint monarchs, of his Protestant daughter Mary and her husband, William of Orange, in 1689. English Whig writers later named it the "Glorious Revolution" because it was said to have been bloodless, to have saved the Protestant religion and to have secured the liberties of Parliament. The question asks whether this praise is deserved, or whether it was also "inglorious", that is, shameful or less admirable in its methods, motives and results. It is argued below that the revolution was glorious in its constitutional achievement and its peaceful course in England, but that it was inglorious in several respects.

**1. Background.** James II became king in 1685. He was a Catholic, he used the royal power to suspend laws and to appoint Catholics to the army, the universities and the government, and he issued Declarations of Indulgence in 1687 and 1688. He was also accused of governing without Parliament. The birth of a Catholic male heir in June 1688, which opened the prospect of a Catholic dynasty, led seven leading men to invite William of Orange, the husband of James's Protestant daughter Mary, to come to England. William landed at Torbay in November 1688, James's army and officers (among them John Churchill) deserted him, and James fled to France in December.

**2. Why it was "glorious".**
- *Largely bloodless in England.* There was no major battle in England, power passed with very little fighting, and there was no civil war as in the 1640s.
- *Defence of Protestantism and liberty.* The revolution ended the fear of a Catholic monarchy and the use of the royal prerogative to dispense with the laws.
- *Constitutional settlement.* In 1689 Parliament offered the crown to William and Mary on condition that they accepted the Declaration of Rights, which became the Bill of Rights in 1689. It declared that the king could not suspend or dispense with laws without Parliament, could not levy taxes or keep a standing army in peacetime without parliamentary consent, that elections and debates in Parliament should be free, that subjects had the right to petition, and that no Catholic could be monarch. The Triennial Act of 1694 required regular elections, and the Act of Settlement of 1701 fixed the Protestant succession and protected the independence of judges.
- *Religious toleration.* The Toleration Act of 1689 allowed most Protestant Dissenters freedom to worship in their own chapels, a step towards religious freedom.
- *Lasting results.* The revolution established that the monarch ruled with the consent of Parliament, ended the claim to rule by divine right, and brought about a constitutional monarchy. Parliament met every year, the financial system developed (for example the Bank of England in 1694), and the philosopher John Locke's ideas on consent and government were influential. The model later inspired political thinkers and revolutionaries in America and elsewhere.

**3. Why it was "inglorious".**
- *A foreign invasion.* William came with a large Dutch fleet and army, so that the change in government was brought about by a foreign force and by the desertion of James's own supporters, rather than by the people of England. The "invitation" came from a small group of nobles, not from the nation.
- *William's motives.* William's main aim was to bring England into his struggle against the France of Louis XIV, which led to the Nine Years' War (1688-97). He acted for the interests of the Dutch Republic as much as for English liberty.
- *A legal fiction and a break in the succession.* Parliament said that James had "abdicated" by fleeing, although he had been driven out, and the rights of his infant son, who was passed over, and of the hereditary principle were set aside. The settlement was a compromise among powerful men. Many Tories were uneasy, a group of clergy refused to swear allegiance to the new rulers (the non-jurors), and Jacobitism, support for the exiled Stuarts, continued, with risings in 1715 and 1745.
- *Violence outside England.* In Ireland the revolution led to war between James II and William, ending in the Williamite victory at the Boyne in 1690 and the Treaty of Limerick in 1691, which was followed by penal laws against Catholics. In Scotland there was fighting at Killiecrankie in 1689, and the massacre of the MacDonalds at Glencoe in 1692 is remembered as a stain on the new regime.
- *Limited reform.* The Toleration Act excluded Catholics and did not extend to those who denied the Trinity, and the Catholic population suffered new restrictions. The settlement benefited the landed aristocracy and gentry in Parliament, not the mass of the people, and the franchise remained very narrow.

**4. Assessment.** For the English political nation the revolution was a great success: it was achieved with little bloodshed and it set Parliament permanently beside the Crown. Its glory, however, was partly a later Whig myth. The change was made by a foreign prince for his own purposes, it involved considerable force and suffering in Ireland and Scotland, and its liberties were limited to a narrow group. It was therefore both glorious and inglorious, depending on whether one looks at its constitutional consequences or at its methods and costs.

**Conclusion.** The view that the 1688 revolution was glorious and inglorious is largely correct. It was glorious in the peaceful change of rulers in England and in the lasting constitutional gains, and inglorious in its dependence on foreign intervention, its compromises and its bloody consequences in Ireland and Scotland.
